title: The environment
hook: stewardship, no waste, water as sacred (6:141; 7:31)

segments.voice: Yesterday, medicine and fasting: the exception for the sick written into the very verse of the fast. Your line was health is a trust. Did you book it, take it, or ask about it? Today the trust gets bigger than one body. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

Who owns the river at the edge of town? The city that bills you for it? The farm upstream that pumps from it? The fish? A verse in the Qur'an doesn't settle the paperwork, but it changes the question. Before humans ever appear on the earth in the story, Allah tells the angels what a person will be. Not an owner. Something else. Today, the environment, and the word for what humans are meant to be in it.
screen: `WHO OWNS THE RIVER?` → `NOT AN OWNER.` → `SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: In Surah al-Baqarah, Pickthall translates the announcement like this: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." The Arabic word is khalifah. A viceroy rules, but in someone else's name. He holds land that isn't his, and he answers for it. So when Muslims speak about the environment, this is where some of them begin: humans as stewards, not owners. Then comes the second idea, no waste. In Surah al-An'am there's a long, almost lush verse about gardens, trellised and untrellised, date palms, olives, pomegranates, crops of every taste. Eat of the fruit, it says, pay what's due on the day of harvest, and don't be wasteful. The same instruction comes back in Surah al-A'raf, this time beside every place of worship: "eat and drink, but be not prodigal. Lo! He loveth not the prodigals." Prodigal is an old word for someone who squanders. Even in plenty, even at a feast, there's a limit. Third, water. In Sunan Abu Dawud the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that Muslims are partners in three things: water, pasture and fire. Shared, in other words. Not something one person can hoard while others go thirsty. And there's a line in Sahih al-Bukhari: if a Muslim plants a tree and a bird, a person or an animal eats from it, it counts for him as charity. A bird. Steward, no waste, shared water, a tree for whoever comes. Put together, it's a quiet picture of what the earth is in this tradition: a trust on loan, with others at the table.
screen: `A VICEROY IN THE EARTH.` · `EAT AND DRINK, BUT BE NOT PRODIGAL.` · `PARTNERS IN WATER, PASTURE AND FIRE.` · `A TREE A BIRD EATS FROM IS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: save water today, starting in your head. Settle, and breathe. Walk back through yesterday and count the taps. The shower. The sink while you brushed. The kettle you filled too full. The dishes. The glass you poured and left. Don't scold yourself. Just see the water moving through your day. Now choose one tap to turn down or off today. If you pray, you can keep the word viceroy in mind: holding something that isn't yours. If you don't, keep the picture of a shared river. The bell holds the time.
The environment. In the Qur'an's picture, the earth is held in trust by a viceroy, eaten from without waste, its water shared. Today's word.
Your line: stewards, not owners. Today, turn one tap off sooner than you usually would, and notice who else that water was for. Tomorrow, green mosques. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Muslim environmental groups and preachers often draw on the idea of humans as khalifah, stewards of the earth, and on the Qur'an's warnings against waste, and some mosques run tree-planting days and water-saving drives.

original.note: Arabic: one who stands in another's place; Pickthall renders it viceroy in 2:30.

trapdoor: what you thought: religion has nothing to say about water bills.
what it means: humans are placed on the earth as stewards, told not to waste even in plenty, and to share water.
what a scholar hears: khalifah in 2:30; the harvest verse in 6:141 and 7:31 against prodigality; the hadith of the three shared things in Abu Dawud and of the tree in al-Bukhari.

sources.ref: Qur'an 6:141 (the gardens; pay the due at harvest; do not waste)
Sunan Abu Dawud 3477 (partners in three: water, pasture and fire)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2320 (a tree whose fruit a bird, person or animal eats is charity)

notes: Confirm Pickthall's wording for 2:30 ('viceroy') and 7:31 exactly as quoted.

Reading khalifah in 2:30 as human stewardship of the earth is a common modern reading; classical commentators also read it as successor to earlier beings or as Adam's line succeeding one another. Confirm the framing 'this is often where they begin'.
'Prodigal is an old word for someone who squanders' is an English gloss, not an etymology of the Arabic.
Confirm hadith numbers: Abu Dawud 3477 (the report speaks of Muslims as partners; classical jurists discuss whether this extends to all people) and Bukhari 2320.
The outline's 'water as sacred' is rendered as 'shared water'; no source is cited for sacredness as such.

Editor: 7:31 was placed 'at the door of the mosque'; Pickthall's verse says 'at every place of worship', so the line now says that. 'Often where they begin' softened to 'where some of them begin'; dropped 'lovely' and 'short' (2:30 is not a short verse).
